submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole fires on grammatical rather than lexical tokens at word boundaries: in Greek on the last character-token of an inflected word - the case/number/person ending - with genitive, plural and feminine nominal suffixes (-εων/-άσεων, -ίας, -ικών/-ικές, -μάτων, -ής, -ης, -ας) and the genitive-plural article των firing hardest, while letters inside a word, word-initial letters and nominative-singular masculine/neuter forms (-ος, -ον, -οι) mostly stay below threshold. In English it is about ten times sparser and fires only on closed-class structural tokens - a determiner directly after 'of', a complementizer ('that') after a noun phrase, an auxiliary or an opening quotation mark right after a comma, and closing punctuation - not on open-class content words.

rival_explanations: A broader word-boundary reading: the pole simply fires at the last token of any word or formatting unit in any language, and its Greek dominance is only an artefact of Greek being tokenized into single characters, so it should also fire on English word-final subword pieces (e.g. 'olecular', 'les') and on one-character Greek words, which this hypothesis predicts are inactive.

A narrower Greek-genitive reading: the pole is only a genitive-plural morpheme detector (-εων/-άσεων/-ων and the article των), with the English, punctuation and -ίας/-ικές/-μάτων/-ουμε firings as unrelated spillover, so it should be inactive on the English 'of the' sites and on the feminine/plural suffixes this hypothesis predicts active.

In this article, we study an elliptic problem involving an operator of mixed order with both local and nonlocal aspects and in the presence of critical nonlinearity of Hartree type. To this end, we first investigate the corresponding Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev inequality and detect the optimal constant. Using variational methods and a Poho\v{z}aev identity we then show the existence and nonexistence results for the corresponding subcritical perturbation problem.

The mixed operator L in (1.1) is given by L = −∆ + (−∆) s for some s ∈ (0, 1). (1. 2) The word "mixed" refers to the type of the operator combining both local and nonlocal features and to the differential order of the operator. The operator L is obtained by the superposition of the classical Laplacian (−∆) and the fractional Laplacian (−∆) s , which for a fixed parameter s ∈ (0, 1), is defined by (−∆) s u = C(n, s)P.V.

These operators model diffusion patterns with different time scales (loosely speaking, the higher order operator leading the diffusion for small scales times and the lower order operator becoming predominant for large times) and they arise for instance in bi-modal power law distribution processes, see [27]. Further applications arise in the theory of optimal searching, biomathematics and animal forging, see [14,15] and the references therein. See also [23,24,28] and the references therein for further applications.

readings.explanation: The pole fires on grammatical rather than lexical tokens at word boundaries: in Greek on the last character-token of an inflected word - the case/number/person ending - with genitive, plural and feminine nominal suffixes (-εων/-άσεων, -ίας, -ικών/-ικές, -μάτων, -ής, -ης, -ας) and the genitive-plural article των firing hardest, while letters inside a word, word-initial letters and nominative-singular masculine/neuter forms (-ος, -ον, -οι) mostly stay below threshold. In English it is about ten times sparser and fires only on closed-class structural tokens - a determiner directly after 'of', a complementizer ('that') after a noun phrase, an auxiliary or an opening quotation mark right after a comma, and closing punctuation - not on open-class content words.

A broader word-boundary reading: the pole simply fires at the last token of any word or formatting unit in any language, and its Greek dominance is only an artefact of Greek being tokenized into single characters, so it should also fire on English word-final subword pieces (e.g. 'olecular', 'les') and on one-character Greek words, which this hypothesis predicts are inactive.

A narrower Greek-genitive reading: the pole is only a genitive-plural morpheme detector (-εων/-άσεων/-ων and the article των), with the English, punctuation and -ίας/-ικές/-μάτων/-ουμε firings as unrelated spillover, so it should be inactive on the English 'of the' sites and on the feminine/plural suffixes this hypothesis predicts active.
